title: A greedy renewal plan as a start

blocks.text: A water utility renews pipe in one-year jobs. Each job $`j`$ has a cost $`c_j`$ ($k, all spent in the year it is done), a value $`v_j`$ ($k), the years $`Y_j`$ it may be done in (earliest first), and a must-do flag. Each year $`y`$ has a budget $`B_y`$. The planners' model has a binary $`x_{j,y}`$ for each job and each $`y \in Y_j`$, at most one year per job (exactly one for a must-do), and one budget row per year. Solves are stopped early on busy nights, so they want a plan in hand from the first moment: a greedy one, handed to the solver as a start.

Before you code, write the greedy rule as an order on the jobs and a placement rule: which jobs come first, how the others are ranked (ties by name), and which year a job takes given the money left in each year, $`B_y - \sum_{j' \text{ placed in } y} c_{j'}`$. A job that fits no year is left out. The must-do jobs come first and are ranked among themselves by the same rule as the others, so when two must-do jobs compete for one year, the one with more value per $k gets it.

items: `greedy_plan(jobs, budget)` returns `{job name: year}` for the jobs the rule places.
`as_hint(x, plan)` turns a plan into a `mathopt.SolutionHint` for the variables `x[(name, year)]`. Give the solver a complete start, as lesson 11.2.1 does.

blocks.text: One test builds the model and asks HiGHS, through MathOpt, whether it accepts your start, by reading its log. About fifteen lines.

"""Run executes this file. Change the calls and see what prints. Submit grades."""
import logging

# Turn the logger up, so the `log.debug` lines of your code show under the printed lines.
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

from ortools.math_opt.python import mathopt

from renewal import Job, as_hint, greedy_plan

years = (2031, 2032)
jobs = [Job("birch", 250, 500, years), Job("cedar", 150, 450, years),
        Job("maple", 300, 400, (2031,), must=True), Job("hazel", 100, 120, years)]
budget = {2031: 450, 2032: 300}

plan = greedy_plan(jobs, budget)
print("greedy plan, budgets 450/300:", plan)

model = mathopt.Model()
x = {(j.name, y): model.add_binary_variable(name=f"x_{j.name}_{y}") for j in jobs for y in j.years}
hint = as_hint(x, plan)
print("hint values set to 1:", sorted(v.name for v, value in hint.variable_values.items() if value == 1.0))
print("hint size:", len(hint.variable_values))

cases.says: the greedy plan keeps every year's budget and funds every must-do job
HiGHS reports the plan, passed as a hint, as a feasible start
optional jobs are ranked by value per $k, not by value alone
a job goes to its earliest year that still has room, not only its first year
must-do jobs take their money before any optional job does
a job that fits no year is skipped and the fill goes on
the start is complete: zeros are given too
two must-do jobs that cannot both fit are ranked by value per $k, like the others
